column3: [p.1, 2, 3] This Environmental Statement for a Marijuana Eradication Project is being submitted

column2: ["Law Enforcement Assistance Administration"]
column3: [p.1, 2, 3] LAW ENFORCEMENT ASSISTANCE ADMINISTRATION FINAL ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT Prepared By: Office of General Counsel Law Enforcement Assistance Administration

column2: The Law Enforcement Assistance Administration proposes a $3,000 grant to spray 65 acres of wild hemp/marijuana fields plus 65 linear miles of ditch and road shoulder in Richgrove Township, Pulaski County, Indiana — a farming community with no towns, growing mainly spearmint and potatoes. A helicopter would apply granulated 2,4-D herbicide (equivalent to 1 lb per acre) in one day in early May. Five alternatives were considered and rejected: burning, mowing, increased police patrols, legalizing marijuana, and doing nothing. The statement calls the overall environmental impact insignificant given the small area, though it acknowledges loss of cover and food for wild birds and changes to insects (including wild bees) and soil microorganisms; the herbicide is described as only slightly toxic to people and animals. Reviewing agencies were generally supportive, with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finding 'no serious impact on the environment' and the Indiana Stream Pollution Control Board believing the herbicide could be applied without direct toxic effect on aquatic life, though residual effects had not been evaluated.
column3: [p.3, 5, 13, 14, 15, 18, 25] The Prosecutor's Office, Winamac, Indiana has requested a $3,000 grant to destroy the marijuana fields in Pulaski County

column2: The Law Enforcement Assistance Administration proposes a $3,000 grant to spray 65 acres of wild hemp/marijuana fields plus 65 linear miles of ditch and road shoulder (20-foot strips on each side) in Richgrove Township, Pulaski County, Indiana. Spraying would be done in one day by helicopter using granulated 2,4-D herbicide (33% acid ester, 67% clay — equivalent to 1 lb 2,4-D per acre) applied in early May when plants are young. The contractor is Clarke Outdoor Spraying Company of La Grange, Illinois.
column3: [p.3, 5] spray 65 square acres and 65 linear miles of ditch and road shoulder with granulated form 2, 4D herbicide

column2: The spray area is in Richgrove Township, Pulaski County, Indiana — a farming community that grows mainly spearmint and potatoes, with no towns or population centers. Two state parks lie nearby (Jasper Pulaski Game Preserve, 7 miles northwest; Winamac Fish and Game Preserve, 8 miles east) but are not expected to be affected. The document also anticipates the project would prevent an influx of roughly 2,000 people coming to pick marijuana.
column3: [p.13, 15] Richgrove Township, Pulaski County is a farmland community, which is predominantly a spearmint and potato growing area.

column2: The statement considers five alternatives and rejects each: (a) burning is infeasible because the muck land would burn continuously and cause air pollution; (b) mowing or tillage cannot reach the inaccessible areas; (c) increased law enforcement patrols would require unavailable personnel and could still stop only about 10% of pickers; (d) legalizing marijuana is outside the agency's authority; and (e) doing nothing (letting the hemp mature) would result in an estimated 200 arrests as pickers are prosecuted.
column3: [p.14, 15] Burning of the Hemp. This is not a feasible alternative since the acreage involved is mostly muck land which would burn continuously and would lead to increased air pollution.

column2: The statement characterizes overall impact as insignificant given the small area. Expected adverse effects include loss of cover and food for wild birds and other fauna, and changes to local insects (including wild bees) and soil microorganisms. The 2,4-D chemical is described as only slightly toxic to people and animals, persisting 7–126 days before being metabolized by soil organisms. Mitigation includes reseeding the area with appropriate cover the same year, using granular (not liquid) form to reduce drift into ditches, spraying by helicopter on a windless day (0–10 mph), and stopping if wind reaches 10 mph. No known irreversible commitment of resources is anticipated.
column3: [p.13, 14, 15, 16, 20] The principal impact on the immediate ecological system will be the loss of cover and food for the wild birds and other fauna which depend on the plants. The loss of these plants will likely also cause changes in the local insect population including any wild bees, and in soil microorganisms.

column2: Reviewing agencies were generally supportive. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency wrote that 2,4-D is registered for wild hemp control and that the program 'will have no serious impact on the environment.' The U.S. Department of Agriculture had no comments. Indiana's Cooperative Extension Service (Purdue) endorsed the single-agency control approach over indiscriminate individual applications. The Indiana Stream Pollution Control Board, after meeting with the contractor, believed the herbicide could be applied without direct toxic effect on aquatic life but noted residual effects had not yet been evaluated. Professor Knake of the University of Illinois urged precautions to keep 2,4-D out of drainage ditches but vouched for the contractor's prior work.
column3: [p.16, 17, 18, 20, 25] The United States Environmental Protection Agency has advised that the 2,4D herbicide proposed use is registered for the control of wild hemp
